summary: Defines L2TP Attribute Value Pair extensions that carry subscriber access line identification and characteristics, as seen at the broadband access server. It also describes a mechanism for carrying this information onward, so the network can know about the customer's line.

eli5.summary: When a home connects through a phone or cable line, the network benefits from knowing details about that line. This note adds fields to a tunneling protocol to pass those details along.

subtitle: Extensions to pass subscriber access line characteristics through broadband tunneling.

tldr.problem: When a home broadband subscriber connects through DSL, cable, or fiber, the broadband access server learns details about the subscriber's line (its speed, capabilities, and type). This information was trapped at the access server and did not reach the network that serves the subscriber.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5515 defines new L2TP Attribute Value Pair (AVP) fields that allow an L2TP Access Concentrator to forward line identification and characterization data (such as actual data rates, minimum rates, interleaving delays, and transmission system type) to the L2TP Network Server. It also defines a mechanism for notifying the server of speed changes during an active session.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now use subscriber line characteristics for authentication, policy decisions, accounting, and troubleshooting without a separate protocol. This enables better service delivery and faster diagnosis of line problems.

today: RFC 5515 is Informational and remains in use. Modern broadband networks rely on L2TP AVP extensions to communicate line characteristics, particularly for DSL and fiber access aggregation, policy enforcement, and service quality monitoring.

sections.title: The Problem of Hidden Line Information
sections.content:
In broadband networks, a DSL Access Multiplexer (DSLAM) or broadband access node terminates subscriber lines and aggregates traffic. The access node knows intimate details about each subscriber's line: its actual speed, whether it supports higher speeds, minimum and maximum speeds configured by the operator, line delay characteristics, and transmission system type (ADSL1, ADSL2, VDSL2, etc.).

However, when the access node tunnels the subscriber's traffic via L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) to a broadband remote access server (BRAS) and then onward to an L2TP Network Server (LNS), this line information has traditionally been unavailable to the LNS and upstream network. The information could be collected from the BRAS and sent to a RADIUS server separately via RFC 4679, but there was no direct mechanism within L2TP itself.

Without access to this line information, the network cannot make fine-grained policy decisions, cannot quickly diagnose why a subscriber's connection is slow, and cannot correlate line quality with subscriber service issues.
sections.eli5: A modem or DSL box knows about the internet line it is using. That information gets lost when the line data is tunneled deeper into the network. This RFC lets the equipment tell everyone else what it knows about the line.

sections.title: L2TP Message Flow: LAC to LNS
sections.content:
The L2TP architecture involves three main components. The Access Node/DSLAM terminates subscriber lines and forwards subscriber identification and line characteristics via one of three methods: vendor-specific PPPoE tags, DHCP relay options, or the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP).

The LAC (L2TP Access Concentrator) runs on the BRAS and receives this line information from the access node. The LAC collects the information and, before establishing an L2TP session with the LNS, forwards the relevant line parameters as new AVPs within the L2TP Incoming-Call-Request (ICRQ) control message.

The LNS (L2TP Network Server) at the network core receives the ICRQ and extracts the line characteristics from the new AVPs. The LNS uses this information for policy decisions, accounting, and management. If the subscriber's line speed changes during the session, the LAC can send updated speed information via new L2TP control messages: Connect-Speed-Update-Notification (CSUN) or Connect-Speed-Update-Request (CSURQ).
sections.eli5: The access equipment learns line facts, tells the BRAS (LAC) about them, and the LAC puts them in an L2TP message going to the network server (LNS). Later, if the line gets faster or slower, the LAC sends an update.

sections.title: Access Line AVP Fields and Values
sections.content:
The RFC defines 19 new Access Line AVPs grouped by category. Identification AVPs include Agent-Circuit-Id (a string identifying the access port on the DSLAM) and Agent-Remote-Id (an operator-configured string, such as a subscriber billing ID).

Data Rate AVPs convey speeds in bits per second: Actual-Data-Rate-Upstream and Downstream (the line's current speeds), Minimum and Maximum data rates (as configured by the operator), and Attainable rates (the highest speeds the line equipment can achieve). Minimum-Data-Rate-Upstream-Low-Power and Downstream-Low-Power convey minimum rates when the line is in low-power states.

Delay AVPs describe interleaving delay in milliseconds: Maximum-Interleaving-Delay-Upstream/Downstream (configured limits), and Actual-Interleaving-Delay-Upstream/Downstream (measured values). Higher interleaving delays trade latency for error correction.

Encapsulation and System Type AVPs specify the physical technology: Access-Loop-Encapsulation (ATM AAL5 or Ethernet, plus layer 2 encapsulation options), ANCP Access Line Type (ADSL1, ADSL2, ADSL2+, VDSL1, VDSL2, SDSL, or unknown), and IWF-Session (whether an Interworking Function transformed ATM to Ethernet).
sections.eli5: The AVPs describe four things about the line: who the subscriber is, how fast it is, how much latency it has, and what type of technology it uses (DSL or fiber, what speeds are possible).

sections.title: Speed Updates During the Session
sections.content:
When a subscriber's line speed changes after the initial L2TP session is established (for example, due to line retraining or a network management action), the LAC can notify the LNS via a new Connect-Speed-Update-Notification (CSUN) message containing a Connect Speed Update AVP. This AVP carries the current transmit and receive speeds for one or more sessions.

To avoid unnecessary message exchanges, the LAC signals its capability to provide speed updates by including a Connect Speed Update Enable AVP in the initial ICRQ. If absent, the LNS knows the LAC will not send updates. The format is different for L2TPv2 (32-bit speed values) and L2TPv3 (64-bit speed values) to support future speed increases.

During failover and resynchronization, the LNS can query the LAC for current speeds of outstanding sessions by sending a Connect-Speed-Update-Request (CSURQ). The LAC MUST respond only for sessions where it previously signaled willingness to send updates.
sections.eli5: If a subscriber's internet gets faster or slower while connected, the LAC can tell the LNS about the change. The LNS can also ask the LAC what the current speed is if the network recovers from a failure.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations and Security
sections.content:
The LAC SHOULD receive line information before session setup to ensure parameters are reliably provided without delaying call setup. If no line information arrives, the LAC establishes the session without waiting but MUST NOT send any Access Line AVPs to the LNS. Local policy determines which information sources (PPPoE, DHCP, ANCP) the LAC prefers; vendors typically default to ANCP.

The LAC MUST be able to filter or limit which AVPs are forwarded to the LNS, as the access node may only provide a subset of available parameters. When information arrives from multiple sources at different times, local policy selects which source to trust.

Security relies on an implied trust relationship between access nodes, the BRAS/LAC, and the LNS. The network infrastructure is assumed to be trusted; identifiers from the access node are accepted without validation. However, AVP values can be hidden using L2TP's AVP-hiding mechanism to protect sensitive subscriber information. No additional security is provided or decreased by these AVPs, but they can be combined with IPsec encryption as described in RFC 3193 for end-to-end tunnel security.
sections.eli5: The system assumes the network equipment from the modem to the server is trustworthy. It expects the LAC to get information about the line before it sets up the tunnel. The LAC can choose which information to forward based on local rules.
